A pun the English Bible cannot keep. Andrewes asks *what is my expectation* and answers *Substantia mea apud te est*, then four lines later *Memorare quæ mea substantia*. Both are the Vulgate — Ps. xxxviii. 8 and lxxxviii. 48 — and both turn on substantia, which is why the two psalms can be set one on top of the other. The Authorised Version renders the first *my hope is in thee* and the second *remember how short my time is*, and the join disappears.

The same half-verse is cited twice in this book under two different numbers. At printed 34 it is *Substantia mea apud te est*, referred to `Psal. xxxix. 7`; here it is the same clause referred to `[Psal. xxxix. 8]`. The difference is the numbering, not the text: xxxix. 7 is the Authorised Version's figure and xxxix. 8 the Prayer Book's, which runs one ahead here. And the Prayer Book's figure is the one in square brackets — the 1853 editor's own mark for a reference he supplied. So the plate cites Andrewes' psalm on the AV's numbering and the editor cites it on the BCP's, on two pages of one book. Both stand as printed.

This is Part II's printed 380 over again in the Harley recension, and the divergences are the whole point. At 380 the plate credits the line in its own running text — *Domine, paratum est cor meum:* *(sic Psaltes, Psal. cviii. 1.)* — so *my heart is ready* is David's, and what follows is *metuo ne meum non sit*, I fear that mine is not. Here the attribution is gone, and so is the *meum*: there is no other man's heart in view, so the psalm's words are spoken in his own voice and simply doubted. And the consolation goes with it. Part II answered the fear with *cupio certe* — I do at least desire — where Part III has only *Utinam esset paratum. Hei mihi quod non est.* A wish and a lament, with the desire taken out. Neither recension is conformed to the other.
